/Issued 133 PM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A significant pattern shift is expected to end the work week and 
through the weekend after a breezy and warm day today. Longwave 
troughing over the Pacific Northwest this afternoon will continue 
to dig south along the western seaboard through Saturday night 
before lifting northeast and over the Northern Rockies through 
Sunday. An embedded wave within the longwave trough will initially 
slide east and over the Northern Rockies through the overnight hours 
tonight and the day on Friday, with a cold front diving south from 
Canada and across Montana during this timeframe. Precipitation will 
accompany the passage of this embedded wave and attendant cold 
front, most notably along and north of the Montana Hwy 200 corridor. 
Additionally, high temperatures will fall into the 50s across the 
plains of Central and North Central Montana on Friday, with the 60s 
to low 70s being observed further south across Southwest Montana 
where the front will arrive later in the day.

By Saturday temperatures will range from the 50s over the plains to 
60s in the valleys of Central and Southwest Montana, with expansive 
cloud cover along and north of the I-90 corridor as Pacific moisture 
streams northeast ahead of the approaching longwave trough. Low 
level north to east upslope flow over Central and North Central 
Montana may support light precipitation across the Island Ranges and 
along the Rocky Mountain Front, with otherwise dry conditions 
expected elsewhere during the day on Saturday.  As better forcing 
arrives Saturday night and on Sunday precipitation will become more 
widespread across Central and North Central Montana, especially 
along west of the I-15 corridor where low to mid-level easterly flow 
will increase. Precipitation is expected to persist through much of 
the day on Sunday, with temperatures struggling to rise into the 40s 
to mid-50s over the plains and upper 50s to low 60s in the valleys. -
 Moldan 

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Lower Elevation Rainfall this Weekend...

Confidence with respect to rainfall amounts, especially along and 
north of the US Hwy 12 corridor, remains low given a high 
variability within the probabilistic data set. This is especially 
true given that "low end", or NBM10Pct values, are zero across all 
of Central and North Central Montana; with even the NBM25Pct values, 
which represent a "reasonable low end" scenario, suggesting a 
scenario in which the entire region see's less than 0.1" of 
rainfall. Ideally for a higher confidence forecast the spread 
between the 25th and 75th ("reasonable high end" scenario) 
percentiles would be closer, but in this case over the plains they 
are generally 0.5" to 1". 

Listed below are NBM5.0 scenarios for "Low End" (NBM10Pct), " Most 
Likely" (NBM50Pct), and "High End" (NBM90Pct) rainfall amounts for 
select locations across North Central, Central, and Southwest 
Montana.

Mountain Snowfall this Weekend...

Confidence is high that the mountains, especially above 6500 feet 
along the Continental Divide north of the Montana Hwy 200 corridor, 
will see snowfall accumulations. Here NBM5.0 10Pct values generally 
range between 0.5" to 1", with some ridgetops across Glacier 
National Park approaching 3". Where uncertainty begins to grow is 
with how low snow levels will ultimately fall with this fall storm, 
along with how much precipitation will ultimately be observed (see 
earlier section). Should precipitation be on the heavier side, 
especially with the initial onset, it is likely that snow levels 
will fall significantly lower to around 5000 feet. Not only will the 
heavier precipitation lead to higher snowfall totals for elevations 
above 6500 feet, with NBM90Pct supporting amounts approaching 6" for 
these elevations, but minor accumulations up to 1" would be possible 
over the high plains adjacent to the Rocky Mountain Front. Given the 
degree of uncertainty that still exists we will hold off on issuing 
any winter weather highlights, but should confidence increase over 
the next 24 hours then a Winter Storm Watch may be warranted given 
the early season impacts to recreation (i.e. hunting season). -
Moldan
